asSun.p: Jupiter rules Sagittarius, and Temperance is Sagittarius's card, so a Sagittarius Sun gets this one handed to it. Your Sun doesn't get any special dignity in Sagittarius. It's a visitor there, neither helped nor held back, and the house it's staying in belongs to Jupiter, which is the planet of more. More room, more meaning, more of everything, and that colours the whole Sun. Which makes it a slightly odd card for you at first glance, because Temperance is about measuring. Have a look at the angel, though. It isn't rationing the water. It's pouring it back and forth between two cups without losing a drop, with one foot on the bank and one in the pool. Sagittarius is mutable fire, fire that moves and changes shape to get where it's going. So what the card says about you is that you try to take in everything and still make something coherent of it, which is harder than it looks, and most of the time you manage.

You collect things. Ideas, places, friends from five different parts of your life who'd never meet unless you threw the party. Then you spend a good part of your life trying to make them fit together into something that means something. At a work lunch you're the one who connects what finance said to what the client said last month, and everyone goes quiet for a second because it's obviously right. At a family dinner you end up translating between your dad and your sister, who agree on a lot and can't hear it. On a Sunday with nothing planned you'll start three books and plan a trip you can't afford, and that's fine, it's how you think. You're honest to the point of blunt, and you're restless. Jupiter makes you want the bigger version of any plan. Temperance is the part of you that, most days, cuts it back to a size you can actually carry.

Sagittarius has a name for blurting, and you've got some of that, but the Temperance version of a Sagittarius Sun has something rarer, which is knowing how much truth a person can take in one go. A friend shows you the business plan they've been working on for a year and it's got a hole in it you could drive a truck through. You don't lie to them. You also don't hand them the whole list. You give them the one thing that matters most, let it settle, and bring up the next one a week later over a drink. People come away from you feeling they've been told the truth and still liked, which most honest people never manage. You're also good at salvage. A plan collapses and by the next morning you've found the part of it worth keeping, and you're already working it into the next one.

The bit nobody warns you about is the preaching. Jupiter is the planet of belief, and once a Sagittarius Sun has found a balanced way of living, a diet, a philosophy, a way of handling money, it can be very hard not to explain it to everybody. Your friend is venting about her boss and you give her a short talk about perspective. She didn't ask for perspective. She wanted you to be cross with her for five minutes. There's a superiority that can creep into being the moderate one, too. You sit above the argument, see both sides, and quietly think less of the two people actually having it. And sometimes the balance is a way of never picking. You keep every option half open, the job and the move and the other job, because choosing one means the others close.

Your first move when things go wrong is to leave, in one sense or another. After a breakup or a bad review or a death in the family, the Sagittarius Sun books something. A drive up the coast, a weekend away, a new course, a gym membership, anything with a horizon in it. You're funny about it in the group chat and you tell everyone it's all for the best. About a week later the running has used up the fuel and it catches up with you, usually late at night, and it comes out as big statements. You're quitting, you're selling up, the whole thing was a mistake. The people close to you get whiplash, because on Monday you were fine and by Friday you're talking about moving to Portugal. What helps is someone who'll come on the drive with you and then, somewhere on the way home, ask how you actually feel.

You love the way you believe in things, completely and a bit out loud. When you're with someone you want to grow with them, take the class together, make the plan for the house or the trip, and you get restless with a partner who seems content to stay exactly where they are. Honesty matters to you in love more than almost anywhere else. You'd sooner hear the hard thing on a Tuesday night than find it out a year later, and you give the same, sometimes before the other person was ready for it. The surprise with this placement is how much steadiness you need from a partner. You'll talk about adventure and mean it, and yet the relationships that last are with someone calm enough to stay put while you come and go, and warm enough that coming home feels good.

You need work that goes somewhere. The job itself can be ordinary, but there has to be a point to it you can say out loud, and when the point goes you lose interest at frightening speed. The ninth house is Sagittarius's natural house, the house of study, travel, publishing, law and belief, so a lot of Sagittarius Suns end up teaching, writing, working across countries, or being the one who explains the strategy to everyone else. You're good at borrowing from other fields. You'll take something you learnt in an old hospitality job and use it to fix a software team's handover, and it works. Where it goes wrong is follow-through. The first seventy percent is exciting and the last thirty is paperwork. Find someone who likes the paperwork and treat them very well.

At twenty a Sagittarius Sun is usually all reach. Three majors, two countries, a lot of opinions and no real idea yet how to mix them, so you swing from one to the next and call it finding yourself. The thirties tend to be when Temperance actually turns up. You've burnt out once or twice by then, overcommitted, overspent, said something too blunt at the wrong wedding, and you start measuring. You travel less and go deeper, and the opinions get fewer and better. The risk in that decade is overcorrecting into a caution that bores you. By the fifties the pattern I see most is a Sagittarius who's become a genuinely good teacher, formally or not, the one younger people bring their big plans to. The thing to watch is telling the same three stories about the year you lived abroad.

Next time you get excited about a plan, a trip, a course, a new way of eating, write it down in full and then cut it in half. Half the budget, half the time, half the scope. Do that version first, properly, all the way to the end. If it goes well you can pour the rest in afterwards. Most Sagittarius Suns find the half-sized version is the one that actually happens, and finishing something small does a lot for their mood.

asMoon.p: The Moon doesn't make light of its own, it reflects the Sun's, and in Sagittarius it's doing that from inside Jupiter's sign. It has no dignity there. It's a guest, neither badly treated nor specially looked after, and the house rules are Jupiter's, which means big feelings and a need for there to be a point to them. Sagittarius is mutable fire. Fire feelings catch fast, and mutable ones change shape quickly too, so your mood can go from flat to lit in an afternoon because someone mentioned a place you've never been. Temperance is Sagittarius's card, and as a Moon card it describes what you do to steady all that. Look at the two cups on the card. The water goes from one to the other and back, and it's the moving that keeps it clear. That's how your feelings settle, by moving them somewhere, talking, walking, mixing a bad mood with a better one until you can live with it again.

You need space around a feeling before you can have it. Somebody asks what's wrong at the dinner table and you honestly don't know yet, you'll know after a walk. When you're anxious your body wants to move, and a long drive with the music up does you more good than an hour of talking. A text left on read doesn't wound you the way it would a water Moon. You assume they're busy, and mostly you're right. Being hemmed in does, though. A weekend where every hour is booked with other people's plans, a partner who wants to know where you are at all times, a flat with no view out of it, and by Sunday night you're scratchy and can't say why. You cheer up at odd things. A plane ticket you won't use for months, an old map, a stranger telling you their life story at a bus stop.

You can feel opposite things at once and not panic about it. That sounds small, but most people can't. At a funeral you're the one who can cry through the eulogy and then laugh properly at the story about the caravan, and you give everyone else in the room permission to do the same. Friends in the middle of a messy divorce come to you because you don't make them pick. They can hate their ex and miss them in the same sentence, and you just nod. Jupiter gives your feelings a generous size, so other people's big emotions don't scare you or make you shrink. The other thing is that you bounce back, and it's real. A bad week leaves a mark and you still wake up on the Saturday curious about something, which is an actual gift to live with.

The trap is turning a feeling into a lesson before you've had it. Something hurts and within the hour you've got a theory about it, what it means, what you've learnt, how it fits into the bigger picture, and you haven't actually cried yet. The theory feels like progress. Often it's a way of standing a few steps back from the pain. The people close to you can find this a bit cold, which surprises you, because you feel anything but cold. The other version is leaving. Closeness that goes on too long without air makes a Sagittarius Moon itchy, and you'll find a reason to be busy, or plan a trip, or pick a small fight about the dishes that gets you out of the room. Your partner wanted to sit on the couch and talk about their mother. You went for a run.

When something goes badly, your mood goes very bright first. You make jokes, you make plans, you tell everyone it'll be fine, and you mostly believe it. The job loss becomes a chance to retrain. The breakup becomes a chance to travel. Some of that is real Jupiter optimism and some of it is outrunning the feeling. About a week later, usually when the plans have stalled, it comes down hard, and a Sagittarius Moon that's low goes quiet and flat in a way that frightens the people used to the bright version. They don't know how to reach you, because you've always been the one who cheers them up. What helps is movement and air before words. A long walk somewhere with a horizon, with one person who doesn't need you to be all right, and the talking tends to come on its own, usually on the way back.

You need to feel free inside a relationship before you can feel safe in it, and that's the part partners often get backwards. Hold on tight and you feel trapped and start pulling away. Leave the door open and you'll probably stay for good. What soothes you is being taken out of the ordinary, a day trip, a new restaurant, a long conversation about something neither of you knows much about. Routine love can feel like being slowly shut in, even when it's kind. With Gemini as Sagittarius's opposite sign, you're often drawn to people who talk a lot, notice details and can keep up. They help more than you'd guess, because they catch the small signs that you're upset before you've clocked them yourself. Tell them early that when you go quiet, a walk together works better for you than a talk across the table.

Your mood at work lives or dies on whether you're learning something. A decent job you've mastered can make you low without you connecting the two, so you come home irritable for six months and blame the commute. You need variety, a bit of travel even if it's only to another office, and colleagues you can have a real conversation with. You also need to believe in the thing, and the moment you catch your employer lying, even about something small, part of you checks out. Honesty is a feeling for you as much as a value. You're good in teams because you lighten a room, and in a bad week you're the one who gets everybody laughing in the kitchen. Be aware that you do that even when you're miserable yourself, and nobody thinks to ask.

A Sagittarius Moon in its twenties is usually restless in a way that looks like fun from outside. You move a lot, change friend groups, fall for people who are going somewhere, and leave when things start to feel ordinary. By the mid-thirties the feelings tend to get more patient. You've found out that the new city came with the same moods as the old one, and you start taking freedom in smaller doses, a weekend away, a class on a Tuesday night, a friend in another country you ring every Sunday. That's Temperance arriving. The fifties often bring the thing you'd never have believed at twenty, a home you love and a real appetite for staying in it, with travel kept for when it means something. The risk later on is getting preachy about how you handled your restless years.

When a feeling lands and you notice yourself reaching for a plan or a theory, give it ten minutes first with your body moving. Walk round the block, no phone, no podcast. Say what the feeling is out loud once, just the word, angry, sad, scared, whichever it is. Then come back and make the plan if you still want to. Most of the time the plan is better for it, and sometimes you find you didn't need one.

asRising.p: Your rising sign was the one coming up on the eastern horizon the minute you were born, and it sets the first house, which is your body, your manner and how you start things. With Sagittarius rising, Jupiter becomes your chart ruler, the planet the whole chart answers to, and Jupiter is the planet of growth, luck, belief and a bit of too much. Temperance is Sagittarius's card, so it's the card strangers meet first. Sagittarius is mutable fire, which on the rising usually shows as warmth that moves. You come across open, quick to laugh, ready to go. Temperance adds a steadiness to that. People expect a Sagittarius rising to be all bounce and then find you listening, weighing things up, taking the heat out of a conversation. In whole-sign houses Gemini sits on your seventh, Virgo on your tenth and Pisces on your fourth, and each of those turns up further down.

Most people decide within a minute that you're easy to talk to. At a wedding where you know nobody, you end up at the table with the bride's grandmother, hearing things her own family hasn't heard. In a job interview you make the panel laugh before the first question, and in a tense meeting you're the one who says the obvious thing everyone was avoiding, in a way that doesn't start a fight. Your instinct in any new situation is to find the common ground fast. You walk in, you read who's at odds with whom, and you start mixing. Physically there's often a looseness to you, a long stride, a habit of standing with one foot already pointed at the door. The flip side is that people assume you're relaxed and fine all the time, when some days you're neither.

Jupiter ruling the chart tends to mean doors open for you through strangers. A conversation in a queue turns into a job. Someone you sat next to on a flight emails a year later with an offer. It isn't magic. You're open with people you don't know, and people who feel met are generous back. The less obvious part is what you do with that luck. The Temperance version of Sagittarius rising passes it on. You're the one who introduces the two friends who should obviously be working together, who mentions a colleague's name in the right meeting, who forwards the job ad to the person who needs it. You mix people. I've seen whole careers and at least a couple of marriages come out of one Sagittarius rising's dinner party, and the host barely noticed.

The easy first impression writes cheques the rest of you then has to cash. You say yes at the door. Yes to the committee, yes to helping them move house, yes to coffee next week with someone you'll never have time for, because in that first warm minute everything seems possible and Jupiter doesn't like saying no. Then the weeks fill up and you let people down in small ways, the late cancellation, the thing you said you'd read and didn't. They're disappointed in proportion to how good the first meeting was. The other shadow is a joke at the wrong moment. You lighten things by instinct, and sometimes a room needed to stay heavy a bit longer. Someone tells you something serious at a barbecue, you reach for a funny line, and you watch their face close.

Under stress your instinct is to go outward. You get more sociable, not less, more jokes, more plans, more people. The boss tells you the project's being cut and within the hour you've rallied the team, organised drinks and floated three new ideas. It works for a while, and the face stays sunny. About a week on it starts showing at home, because Pisces sits on your fourth house, and that's where whatever you didn't deal with goes to pool. You get vague and tired there, drift through the evening on your phone, can't decide what to eat. Your partner or housemate gets the foggy version and nobody else does. What helps is admitting it at the front door as well as the back one. Tell one colleague or friend it's been a rotten week, and give yourself an evening at home with nothing to steer.

With Sagittarius rising, Gemini lands on your seventh house, the house of partners, and the people you end up with are very often talkers. Clever, curious, a bit scattered, the kind who send you an article at midnight. That's The Lovers sitting across the chart from Temperance, and it tends to make a relationship one long conversation. At first the pull is easy. You make a good first impression, you're fun on a date, and people fall for the open, adventurous version of you quite fast. The trouble comes when a partner starts wanting the details. Where were you, what did you mean, why did you say that to my sister. Sagittarius rising prefers the headline, and Gemini on the seventh keeps asking for the small print. Stay for that. The partners who make you explain yourself usually end up knowing you best.

Virgo sits on your tenth house, the house of career and reputation, which is a funny combination with a Sagittarius front. You walk in looking like the big-picture person, and what you end up known for professionally is often care with detail, craft, fixing things properly. People hire the enthusiasm and keep you for the accuracy. Virgo and Sagittarius are square to each other, two mutable signs pulling different ways, so there's friction here you feel most weeks. Part of you wants to pitch the vision and part of you wants to check the numbers three times. Temperance is how you live with that. Pitch in the morning, check in the afternoon, and don't let either one have the whole day. You also do well anywhere first contact matters, sales, teaching, hospitality, being the face of a small business.

Sagittarius rising at twenty often gets taken for older, braver and more sorted than they are, because the manner is so easy. You get invited to everything and say yes to all of it, and you can be a bit careless with people because there always seem to be plenty more of them. Through the thirties the Virgo tenth tends to start earning its keep. A reputation builds around what you actually deliver, and the easy manner becomes useful as well as charming. You learn to promise less at the door. By the fifties I usually see a Sagittarius rising who's become the one everybody wants at the table, the host, the mentor, the person who gets strangers talking. The body tends to ask for a slower pace around then, knees and back mostly, and it's worth going along with it early.

Before you say yes to anything at a first meeting, a favour, a project, a coffee, say 'let me check and I'll text you tonight'. Then actually check. Look at the week, ask yourself whether you want it, and send the text, yes or no. The Sagittarius rising warmth survives a short delay perfectly well, and people remember the ones who kept their word for a long time after they've forgotten who said yes quickly.

asBirthCard.p: This one comes from your birthdate, not your chart. Add every digit of the date together, and if the total is over 22, add those digits again. Yours lands on 14, either straight away or by way of 59, and 14 is Temperance. Fourteen is seven doubled, and seven is The Chariot, the card of driving hard in one direction. Double it and you get the card that has learnt to hold both directions at once. It sits straight after Death, card 13, which is the ending, and just before The Devil, card 15, which is getting stuck in something. So Temperance is the stretch in between, where you rebuild after a loss and find a way of living that doesn't tip into excess. The card's own sign is Sagittarius, fire ruled by Jupiter, so there's a hopeful streak in its nature. That's the card talking, and it holds whatever your Sun sign happens to be.

As a lifelong pattern, fourteen shows up as being put in the middle. You're the one standing between two people, two cultures, two jobs, two versions of what the family wants from you. Maybe your parents split when you were young and you carried messages between the houses. Maybe at work you're the one who translates between the engineers and the sales team. At a wedding you get seated between the two cousins who aren't speaking, and by dessert they're at least passing the salt. You also keep arriving after something. After a redundancy, after an illness, after someone's moved out, and your job is making a life out of what remains. You probably know a lot about starting again halfway through, for someone your age, and you don't think of it as a skill, though it is one.

People tend to call you when the flowers have stopped arriving. You're good at the long, dull middle of recovery, the second month after the funeral, the third round of physio, the year after the divorce when everyone else has moved on and the person is still putting their life back together. You don't need drama to stay interested, and you don't hurry anybody. You drop off soup and ask how the sleep's been and mean it. The same thing works on yourself, which is less common. You can take a bad stretch in small doses, a bit of work, a bit of rest, a bit of company, and put yourself back together without a big turning point. Friends who've been through something hard often say afterwards that you were the one who stayed, and you probably didn't notice you were doing it.

Standing in the middle for years can leave you without a side of your own. You're so used to translating for everyone else that when someone asks what you want for dinner, let alone from your life, there's a pause where the answer should be. At family gatherings you manage everybody's moods and come home without having said one thing you actually think. The other risk sits next door. The Devil is card 15, one step on, and moderation can quietly turn into a set of rules you can't break, the careful diet, the strict budget, the one glass and never two, until the balance itself is the thing you're hooked on. It looks healthy from outside, and some of it is. It's gone too far when one late night or one blown budget ruins your whole week.

Pressure pushes a fourteen towards controlling the mixture. Something goes wrong, the diagnosis, the money, the relationship, and the first thing you do is try to rebalance everything at once. New routine, new budget, early nights, a spreadsheet for the week. For a few days it genuinely helps. About a week later the effort of keeping every cup level wears you down, and the swing comes, the bottle of wine or the online shopping at 2am or the whole weekend in bed, then the guilt, then a stricter routine to make up for it. The people around you watch the see-saw and aren't sure which version they'll get on Friday. What helps is letting something stay unbalanced on purpose for a while. Pick the one area that really matters, look after that, and let the rest be messy.

Relationships for a fourteen tend to be about joining two whole lives, and you're more aware than most of how much work that is. Two sets of friends, two ways of doing Christmas, two ideas about money. You're good at it, patient about it, and you don't expect the fit to be instant. What catches people with this card is that they often become the one who adjusts. You learn your partner's family's jokes, their music, their way of loading the dishwasher, and a few years in you can't find much of your own flavour left in the mix. A good partner for you is someone who notices that and asks for more of you, the opinions, the old friends, the food you grew up on. If you're with someone who's never once had to change to fit you, have a look at that.

Your working life tends to have seams in it. A career change at thirty-five, two jobs at once, a trade and a degree, a role that's half technical and half people. That's the number at work, and it's worth not apologising for it on your CV, because it's usually your edge. You're the person who can sit between departments or professions and make them understand each other, the nurse who became a manager, the chef who teaches. You also have a feel for pacing. You know when to add a bit more pressure and when the team needs a slow week, and good managers notice that about you. What wears you down is work that allows only one mode, all sprint or all routine. If a job has been one flavour for too long, change one ingredient before you think about leaving it.

In your twenties the fourteen pattern often looks like being pulled between things, and it can feel like indecision. Two cities, two courses, two people, and you feel slightly behind the friends who just picked. Somewhere in the thirties there tends to be a loss or an ending, the Death card sitting right behind this one, and what you build afterwards is the first thing that feels properly yours, made from everything that came before. That's when the pattern starts making sense. By the fifties most people with this birth card have a reputation for steadiness and a life with a lot of different pieces in it that somehow fit. The thing to watch later is getting so settled in the balance that you stop adding anything new. Take the class, go on the trip with the friend you've only just met, cook something you've never tasted.

Once a week, pick one thing in your life that's gone to an extreme, either too much of it or none at all. Too much work and no reading, all the socialising at weekends and none midweek, whatever it is. Move it one notch towards the middle and only one. Half an hour less at the desk on Wednesday. One phone call to a friend on a Tuesday. Keep that single change for the week and see how it sits before you touch anything else.
